pairs.source_text: Si minor Atrides Helenen, Helenesque sororem Quo premat Atrides crimine maior habet,
pairs.question: Cuius soror erat coniunx illa scelesta quam Atrides maior Agamemnon habuit?
pairs.question_en: Whose sister was that guilty wife whom the elder Atrides, Agamemnon, had?
pairs.derivation: Kinship fact: Clytemnestra was Helen's sister — the two Atridae married the two sisters. 'Helenesque sororem... Atrides... maior' verbatim; canonical genealogy.

pairs.source_text: Si scelere Oeclides Talaioniae Eriphylae Vivus et in vivis ad Styga venit equis,
pairs.question: Cuius uxoris scelere Oeclides Amphiaraus vivus cum equis ad Styga descendit?
pairs.question_en: By whose wifely crime did Amphiaraus, son of Oecles, go down alive with his horses to the Styx?
pairs.derivation: The seer Amphiaraus ('Oeclides'), betrayed by Eriphyle (bribed with the necklace), swallowed alive with chariot and horses — canonical Theban-war story. Both identifications verbatim ('Oeclides... Eriphylae... vivus... ad Styga... equis').

pairs.source_text: Est pia Penelope lustris errante duobus Et totidem lustris bella gerente viro.
pairs.question: Per quot lustra vir Penelopae bella gessit, et per quot erravit?
pairs.question_en: For how many lustra did Penelope's husband wage war, and for how many did he wander?
pairs.derivation: The canonical arithmetic of Ulysses' absence — ten years of war, ten of wandering — counted by Ovid in lustra (five-year periods), while Penelope stayed 'pia'. Number fact, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Respice Phylaciden et quae comes isse marito Fertur et ante annos occubuisse suos.
pairs.question: Quae uxor Phylacidae Protesilai comes in mortem isse ante annos suos fertur?
pairs.question_en: Which wife of Protesilaus of Phylace is said to have followed her husband in death before her time?
pairs.derivation: Laodamia dying to accompany Protesilaus ('Phylacides', the man of Phylace, first Greek to fall at Troy) — canonical exemplum of wifely devotion; Ovid names her at 3.138. 'Fertur' keeps the story-frame.

pairs.source_text: Fata Pheretiadae coniunx Pagasaea redemit: Proque viro est uxor funere lata viri.
pairs.question: Quae uxor fata Admeti Pheretiadae morte sua redemit?
pairs.question_en: Which wife redeemed the fate of Admetus, son of Pheres, by her own death?
pairs.derivation: Alcestis, the 'Pagasaean (Thessalian) wife', dying in place of Admetus ('Pheretiades', son of Pheres) — canonical exemplum; the substitution-death is verbatim ('proque viro est uxor funere lata viri').

pairs.source_text: 'Accipe me, Capaneu! cineres miscebimus' inquit Iphias, in medios desiluitque rogos.
pairs.question: Cuius mariti in medios rogos Iphias Evadne desiluit?
pairs.question_en: Onto whose funeral pyre did Evadne, daughter of Iphis, leap?
pairs.derivation: Evadne ('Iphias', daughter of Iphis) leaping onto the pyre of her husband Capaneus — canonical devotion exemplum; Capaneus named verbatim, 'cineres miscebimus' the famous cry.

pairs.locus: Ovid, Ars Amatoria 3.37-38 (Phyllis et Novem viae)
pairs.source_text: Quaere, novem cur una viae dicantur, et audi Depositis silvas Phyllida flesse comis.
pairs.question: Ob quam puellam locus ille Threicius 'Novem viae' dictus est, quam silvae depositis comis fleverunt?
pairs.question_en: For which girl was the Thracian place called the 'Nine Ways' named, whom the woods mourned by shedding their leaves?
pairs.derivation: The aition of Ennea Hodoi ('Novem viae') in Thrace, tied to Phyllis' nine runs to the shore awaiting Demophoon, and the leaf-shedding mourning of the woods. Both aition and name verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Et famam pietatis habet, tamen hospes et ensem Praebuit et causam mortis, Elissa, tuae.
pairs.question: Quis hospes, pietatis fama notus, Elissae Didoni ensem causamque mortis praebuit?
pairs.question_en: Which guest, famed for his piety, furnished Elissa (Dido) with the sword and the cause of her death?
pairs.derivation: Dido ('Elissa', her Phoenician name, verbatim) dying by the sword of the guest 'famed for pietas' — the periphrasis can only be pius Aeneas. Canonical Aeneid fact seen from Ovid's angle.

pairs.source_text: Probra Therapnaeae qui dixerat ante maritae, Mox cecinit laudes prosperiore lyra.
pairs.question: Quis poeta, cum probra Helenae dixisset, mox laudes eius felicioribus modis cecinit?
pairs.question_en: Which poet, having first spoken abuse of Helen, soon sang her praises in a happier strain?
pairs.derivation: The famous palinode of Stesichorus, who abused the 'Therapnaean wife' (Helen of Therapne near Sparta), was struck blind, and recanted with praises. Ovid gives the periphrasis; the identification is the celebrated literary anecdote (Plato, Phaedrus 243a).

pairs.source_text: Dixit, et e myrto (myrto nam vincta capillos Constiterat) folium granaque pauca dedit;
pairs.question: Qua fronde Venus capillos vincire solet?
pairs.question_en: With what foliage does Venus customarily bind her hair?
pairs.derivation: The myrtle as Venus' sacred plant — she appears to Ovid with hair bound in myrtle and gives him a myrtle leaf and berries. Canonical attribute, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Latmius Endymion non est tibi, Luna, rubori, Nec Cephalus roseae praeda pudenda deae.
pairs.question: Quem iuvenem Latmium Luna amavit?
pairs.question_en: Which youth of Latmos did the Moon love?
pairs.derivation: Luna and Endymion of Mount Latmos — canonical divine love; both names verbatim ('Latmius Endymion... tibi, Luna').

pairs.source_text: Latmius Endymion non est tibi, Luna, rubori, Nec Cephalus roseae praeda pudenda deae.
pairs.question: Cuius deae praeda fuit Cephalus?
pairs.question_en: Of which goddess was Cephalus the prize?
pairs.derivation: Cephalus carried off by the 'rosy goddess' — the dawn-goddess Aurora, her canonical epithet fixing the referent. Prepares the Cephalus-Procris story told at the book's end.

pairs.source_text: Ut Veneri, quem luget adhuc, donetur Adonis: Unde habet Aenean Harmoniamque suos?
pairs.question: Quam filiam Venus suam habuit, ut cum Aenea filio Ovidius commemorat?
pairs.question_en: Which daughter did Venus have as her own, whom Ovid names beside her son Aeneas?
pairs.derivation: Venus' children Aeneas and Harmonia (her daughter by Mars) — the Harmonia link is the fact taken; Aeneas-Venus parentage is already in the Fasti 4 file. Verbatim 'Aenean Harmoniamque suos'.

pairs.source_text: Curia, concilio quae nunc dignissima tanto, De stipula Tatio regna tenente fuit.
pairs.question: Quo rege regna tenente curia Romana de stipula facta erat?
pairs.question_en: Under which king's reign was the Roman senate-house made of straw?
pairs.derivation: The primitive straw curia in the days of (Titus) Tatius, Romulus' Sabine co-king — Ovid's emblem of old Rome against the marble present. Both facts verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quae nunc sub Phoebo ducibusque Palatia fulgent, Quid nisi araturis pascua bubus erant?
pairs.question: In quo colle Romano et templum Phoebi et domus principum aetate Ovidii fulgebant?
pairs.question_en: On which Roman hill did both the temple of Phoebus and the house of the leaders shine in Ovid's day?
pairs.derivation: The Palatine 'gleaming under Phoebus and the leaders' — Apollo's Palatine temple beside the house of Augustus, on ground once mere ox-pasture. Topographical fact verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Simplicitas rudis ante fuit: nunc aurea Roma est, Et domiti magnas possidet orbis opes.
pairs.question: Quo epitheto celeberrimo Ovidius Romam sui temporis appellat?
pairs.question_en: By what famous epithet does Ovid call the Rome of his own day?
pairs.derivation: 'Nunc aurea Roma est' — the quotable tag for Augustan Rome enriched by the conquered world. Proverb-famous phrase; the checkable point (whose phrase, of what city) is verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Vos quoque nec caris aures onerate lapillis, Quos legit in viridi decolor Indus aqua,
pairs.question: Quis lapillos caros, quibus aures Romanae onerabantur, in viridi aqua legebat?
pairs.question_en: Who gathered in green waters the costly pearls with which Roman ears were laden?
pairs.derivation: Pearls as Indian imports, dived for by the 'decolor Indus' — the luxury-trade fact behind Roman earrings. Verbatim; geography of commerce.

pairs.source_text: Sed neque ramosa numerabis in ilice glandes, Nec quot apes Hyblae, nec quot in Alpe ferae, Nec mihi tot positus numero conprendere fas est: Adicit ornatus proxima quaeque dies.
pairs.question: Quot positus capillorum feminis Romanis fuisse Ovidius ait?
pairs.answer: Innumerabiles; novos ornatus quisque dies adicit.
pairs.question_en: How many hairstyles does Ovid say Roman women had?
pairs.answer_en: Countless; each new day adds new fashions.
pairs.derivation: The famous claim that coiffures are as countless as acorns, Hybla's bees, or Alpine beasts, 'each next day adding new modes' — the cultural fact of Roman hairstyle profusion, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Longa probat facies capitis discrimina puri: Sic erat ornatis Laodamia comis.
pairs.question: Quo capillorum ornatu Laodamia usa esse dicitur apud Ovidium?
pairs.question_en: With what hair-arrangement is Laodamia said, in Ovid, to have been adorned?
pairs.answer_en: With a plain parting (a simple central division).
pairs.derivation: The named-style fact from the coiffure taxonomy: the plain central parting (suited to a long face) is Laodamia's canonical style. Verbatim; attributed to Ovid.

pairs.source_text: Altera succinctae religetur more Dianae, Ut solet, attonitas cum petit illa feras.
pairs.question: Quo habitu Diana feras petere solet?
pairs.question_en: In what garb does Diana customarily hunt wild beasts?
pairs.answer_en: Girt up, with her hair bound back.
pairs.derivation: The canonical iconography of the huntress Diana — tunic girt up, hair tied back — cited as the model for one hairstyle. Verbatim ('succinctae... more Dianae').

pairs.source_text: Alterius crines umero iactentur utroque: Talis es adsumpta, Phoebe canore, lyra.
pairs.question: Quo capillorum habitu Phoebus, cum lyram tenet, fingi solet?
pairs.question_en: With what hair is Phoebus represented when he holds the lyre?
pairs.answer_en: With locks flung loose over both shoulders.
pairs.derivation: The canonical image of the unshorn lyre-god: Apollo's hair streaming over both shoulders, cited as the model for a loose style. Verbatim ('crines umero... utroque: talis es... Phoebe... lyra').

pairs.source_text: Ars casum simulat; sic capta vidit ut urbe Alcides Iolen, 'hanc ego' dixit 'amo.'
pairs.question: Quam virginem Alcides Hercules, urbe eius capta, visam amavit?
pairs.question_en: Which maiden did Hercules (Alcides) see and love when her city was captured?
pairs.derivation: Hercules falling for Iole at the sack of Oechalia — canonical late-Hercules story ('capta... urbe Alcides Iolen... amo'). Both names verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Femina canitiem Germanis inficit herbis, Et melior vero quaeritur arte color:
pairs.question: Quibus herbis feminae Romanae canitiem inficiebant?
pairs.question_en: With what herbs did Roman women dye their gray hair?
pairs.derivation: Hair-dye realia: graying hair colored with 'German herbs' (the famous Rhenish soaps and dyes that gave the reddish-blond shade). Verbatim; toilette culture, not advice.

pairs.source_text: Femina procedit densissima crinibus emptis, Proque suis alios efficit aere suos.
pairs.question: Quo modo feminae Romanae raros capillos densabant?
pairs.answer: Crinibus emptis (alienis pro suis aere paratis).
pairs.question_en: How did Roman women thicken their thinning hair?
pairs.answer_en: With purchased hair (others' locks bought for money as their own).
pairs.derivation: Wig-realia: bought hair worn openly, 'making others' hair one's own for cash' — the wig trade as everyday fact, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nec rubor est emisse; palam venire videmus Herculis ante oculos virgineumque chorum.
pairs.question: Ante quorum numinum oculos crines empticii Romae palam venibant?
pairs.question_en: Before the eyes of which divinities was purchased hair openly sold at Rome?
pairs.answer_en: Of Hercules and the maiden band of the Muses.
pairs.derivation: The hair-market held 'before the eyes of Hercules and the virgin chorus' — by the temple of Hercules Musarum (in the Circus Flaminius quarter). Shopping topography verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid de veste loquar? Nec vos, segmenta, requiro Nec te, quae Tyrio murice, lana, rubes.
pairs.question: Quo animali marino lana Tyria rubebat?
pairs.question_en: From what sea-creature did Tyrian wool get its red?
pairs.derivation: Tyrian purple dyed with the murex shellfish — the canonical luxury-dye fact ('Tyrio murice, lana, rubes'), dismissed by Ovid in favor of cheaper colors.

pairs.source_text: Ecce, tibi similis, quae quondam Phrixon et Hellen Diceris Inois eripuisse dolis;
pairs.question: Quos fratres aries ille aureus Inois dolis eripuisse dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Which brother and sister is the golden ram said to have snatched from the wiles of Ino?
pairs.derivation: The golden-fleece ram rescuing Phrixus and Helle from their stepmother Ino's plots — canonical myth, here the referent of a wool-color's name. All three names verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Ille crocum simulat: croceo velatur amictu, Roscida luciferos cum dea iungit equos:
pairs.question: Quae dea, croceo amictu velata, luciferos equos iungit?
pairs.question_en: Which goddess, veiled in a saffron cloak, yokes the light-bringing horses?
pairs.derivation: The dawn-goddess in her canonical saffron robe ('croceo... amictu') yoking the horses of the light — the epic epithet crocea Aurora, here explaining the saffron dress-color. Periphrasis with one referent.

pairs.source_text: Pulla decent niveas: Briseida pulla decebant: Cum rapta est, pulla tum quoque veste fuit.
pairs.question: Quali veste Briseis, cum ab Achille rapta est, fuit, ut Ovidius refert?
pairs.question_en: In what sort of dress was Briseis when she was carried off, as Ovid relates?
pairs.derivation: Ovid's mythographic detail that dark-clad Briseis was seized in mourning dress — author-particular claim, hence attributed; 'pulla tum quoque veste' verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Alba decent fuscas: albis, Cephei, placebas: Sic tibi vestitae pressa Seriphos erat.
pairs.question: Cuius regis filia erat Andromeda, quae fusca albis vestibus placebat?
pairs.question_en: Which king's daughter was Andromeda, the dark beauty who pleased in white garments?
pairs.derivation: Andromeda addressed as 'Cephei' (daughter of Cepheus) — kinship fact verbatim; her dark skin and the Seriphos setting (where Perseus brought her) frame the color-advice, which is dropped.

pairs.source_text: Quid si praecipiam ne fuscet inertia dentes, Oraque suscepta mane laventur aqua?
pairs.question: Quo tempore diei ora aqua lavari solebant, ut Ovidius pro re nota commemorat?
pairs.question_en: At what time of day was the face customarily washed with water, as Ovid mentions as a matter of course?
pairs.derivation: The morning toilet: face washed with water at daybreak, cited by Ovid as too obvious to need teaching — which is what makes it shared daily-life custom. Verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quid si praecipiam ne fuscet inertia dentes, Oraque suscepta mane laventur aqua?
pairs.question: Qua re dentes fuscari Ovidius dicit, nisi cura adhibetur?
pairs.question_en: By what does Ovid say teeth are blackened, if care is not taken?
pairs.derivation: Teeth-cleaning as daily practice: only 'inertia' lets teeth darken — i.e., regular rubbing of the teeth was assumed. The custom-fact behind the aside; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Scitis et inducta candorem quaerere creta: Sanguine quae vero non rubet, arte rubet.
pairs.question: Qua re inducta feminae Romanae candorem cutis quaerebant?
pairs.question_en: By applying what did Roman women seek a fair complexion?
pairs.derivation: Cosmetics realia: whitening with applied chalk, and artificial rouge for those with no natural color ('arte rubet'). Verbatim; practice-fact, not advice.

pairs.source_text: Nec pudor est oculos tenui signare favilla, Vel prope te nato, lucide Cydne, croco.
pairs.question: Quibus rebus feminae Romanae oculos signare solebant?
pairs.question_en: With what did Roman women outline their eyes?
pairs.answer_en: With fine ash or with saffron.
pairs.derivation: Eye-makeup realia: eyes marked with fine ash (soot) or saffron. Verbatim; the toilet practice, culturally salient (cf. the Medicamina).

pairs.source_text: Nec pudor est oculos tenui signare favilla, Vel prope te nato, lucide Cydne, croco.
pairs.question: Prope quod flumen lucidum crocus ille laudatus nascitur, ut Ovidius ait?
pairs.question_en: Near what clear river does the famed saffron grow, as Ovid says?
pairs.derivation: The best saffron grown by the Cydnus in Cilicia (the Corycian crocus of the poets) — product-geography verbatim ('prope te nato, lucide Cydne, croco').

pairs.source_text: Est mihi, quo dixi vestrae medicamina formae, Parvus, sed cura grande, libellus, opus;
pairs.question: Quid Ovidius de medicaminibus formae feminarum se composuisse ait?
pairs.question_en: What does Ovid say he composed on the beauty-treatments of women's looks?
pairs.derivation: Ovid's self-reference to his own cosmetic poem, the Medicamina Faciei Femineae — literary-historical fact about the poet's works, stated verbatim ('medicamina formae, parvus... libellus').

pairs.source_text: Oesypa quid redolent? quamvis mittatur Athenis Demptus ab inmundo vellere sucus ovis.
pairs.question: Unde oesypum, sucus ab inmundo vellere ovium demptus, Romam mittebatur?
pairs.question_en: From where was oesypum, the grease taken from unwashed sheep's fleece, sent to Rome?
pairs.derivation: Oesypum, the lanolin skin-cosmetic extracted from raw fleece, imported from Athens — two realia (what it is, whence it came) both verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quae nunc nomen habent operosi signa Myronis Pondus iners quondam duraque massa fuit;
pairs.question: Qua arte clarus erat Myron, cuius nomen signa operosa ferunt?
pairs.question_en: In what art was Myron famous, whose name his elaborate statues bear?
pairs.derivation: Myron the canonical Greek sculptor, byword for masterworks ('operosi signa Myronis') — art-culture knowledge every Roman carried; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cum fieret, lapis asper erat: nunc, nobile signum, Nuda Venus madidas exprimit imbre comas.
pairs.question: Quid Venus in nobili illo signo facere fingitur?
pairs.question_en: What is Venus represented doing in that famous statue?
pairs.answer_en: Naked, she wrings her hair wet with the sea-spray.
pairs.derivation: The celebrated Venus Anadyomene type (after Apelles): the nude goddess wringing her sea-wet hair — 'nobile signum' verbatim. Art-culture fact of the shared visual canon.

pairs.source_text: Aurea quae splendent ornato signa theatro, Inspice, contemnes: brattea ligna tegit;
pairs.question: Quid sub aureis signis, quae in theatro Romano splendent, revera latet?
pairs.question_en: What really lies beneath the golden statues that gleam in the Roman theater?
pairs.derivation: Theater-decor realia: the 'golden' statues are gilt wood ('brattea ligna tegit') — a spectacle-culture fact Ovid uses as a simile for cosmetic art. Verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tuta sit ornatrix; odi, quae sauciat ora Unguibus et rapta brachia figit acu.
pairs.question: Quo nomine vocabatur ancilla quae dominae Romanae capillos componebat?
pairs.question_en: By what name was the slave-girl called who dressed a Roman lady's hair?
pairs.derivation: The ornatrix, the lady's hairdresser — named verbatim, with the realia of mistresses scratching her face and stabbing her arm with the hairpin (which Ovid condemns). Household daily life.

pairs.source_text: Quae male crinita est, custodem in limine ponat, Orneturve Bonae semper in aede deae.
pairs.question: In cuius deae aede mulierem male crinitam tuto ornari posse Ovidius iocatur, quod viri inde arcentur?
pairs.question_en: In which goddess's temple does Ovid joke that a woman with bad hair may safely dress, since men are barred from it?
pairs.derivation: The temple of Bona Dea, from whose rites and precinct men were excluded — the point of Ovid's joke about dressing where no male eye can see. Goddess named verbatim; the exclusion is the canonical fact the joke presupposes (cf. the Clodius scandal).

pairs.source_text: Conveniunt tenues scapulis analemptrides altis: Angustum circa fascia pectus eat.
pairs.question: Quo vinculo pectus feminae Romanae sub veste cingebatur?
pairs.question_en: With what band was a Roman woman's chest bound beneath her dress?
pairs.derivation: The fascia pectoralis, the Roman breast-band ('angustum circa fascia pectus eat'), beside the shoulder-pads (analemptrides) for high shoulder-blades — dress realia verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Monstra maris Sirenes erant, quae voce canora Quamlibet admissas detinuere rates.
pairs.question: Qua re Sirenes, monstra maris, rates transeuntes detinebant?
pairs.question_en: By what did the Sirens, monsters of the sea, detain the passing ships?
pairs.derivation: The Sirens as sea-monsters whose song stopped any ship — canonical Odyssey lore stated as a definition. Verbatim.

pairs.source_text: His sua Sisyphides auditis paene resolvit Corpora, nam sociis inlita cera fuit.
pairs.question: Qua re aures sociorum Ulixis contra cantum Sirenum munitae erant?
pairs.question_en: With what were the ears of Ulysses' companions sealed against the Sirens' song?
pairs.derivation: The wax in the comrades' ears while bound Ulysses ('Sisyphides' — the taunt that Sisyphus begot him) nearly broke free — canonical episode, verbatim ('sociis inlita cera').

pairs.source_text: Saxa ferasque lyra movit Rhodopeius Orpheus, Tartareosque lacus tergeminumque canem.
pairs.question: Quae Orpheus Rhodopeius lyra sua movit?
pairs.answer: Saxa ferasque, atque ipsos inferos (lacus Tartareos canemque).
pairs.question_en: What did Orpheus of Rhodope move with his lyre?
pairs.answer_en: Rocks and wild beasts, and the underworld itself (the Tartarean lakes and the dog).
pairs.derivation: The canonical powers of Orpheus' lyre: rocks, beasts, and the powers below. Verbatim; 'Rhodopeius' fixes his Thracian home.

pairs.source_text: Saxa ferasque lyra movit Rhodopeius Orpheus, Tartareosque lacus tergeminumque canem.
pairs.question: Quot capita canis ille Tartareus Cerberus habet, quem 'tergeminum' Ovidius vocat?
pairs.question_en: How many heads has Cerberus, the dog of Tartarus, whom Ovid calls 'threefold'?
pairs.derivation: Cerberus 'tergeminus' — the three-headed hound of the underworld, canonical attribute stated verbatim in the epithet.

pairs.source_text: Saxa tuo cantu, vindex iustissime matris, Fecerunt muros officiosa novos.
pairs.question: Cuius cantu saxa sponte coeuntia muros Thebanos novos fecerunt?
pairs.question_en: At whose song did the stones, moving of themselves, build the new walls of Thebes?
pairs.derivation: Amphion, addressed as 'most just avenger of his mother' (Antiope), whose lyre-song charmed the stones into Thebes' walls — canonical identification of the periphrasis; the wall-building fact verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sit tibi Callimachi, sit Coi nota poetae, Sit quoque vinosi Teia Musa senis;
pairs.question: Quis poeta, 'vinosus senex' cuius Musa Teia est, in indice legendorum Ovidii ponitur?
pairs.question_en: Which poet, the 'wine-loving old man' whose Muse is Teian, stands in Ovid's reading list?
pairs.derivation: Anacreon of Teos, the wine-poet — 'vinosi Teia Musa senis' is his canonical periphrasis in the famous reading list for girls (with Callimachus and the Coan). Literary-canon fact.

pairs.source_text: Sit tibi Callimachi, sit Coi nota poetae, Sit quoque vinosi Teia Musa senis;
pairs.question: Quis poeta Cous, cum Callimacho legendus, elegiae Graecae auctor celebratur?
pairs.question_en: Which Coan poet, to be read alongside Callimachus, is celebrated as a master of Greek elegy?
pairs.derivation: 'The Coan poet' paired with Callimachus is Philitas — the standard elegiac canon-pair (so too Propertius 3.1). The periphrasis has one canonical referent; reading-list fact.

pairs.source_text: Nota sit et Sappho (quid enim lascivius illa?), Cuive pater vafri luditur arte Getae.
pairs.question: Quae poetria in indice legendorum Ovidii nota esse debet, qua nihil lascivius esse ait?
pairs.question_en: Which poetess must be known, in Ovid's reading list, than whom he says nothing is more wanton?
pairs.derivation: Sappho in the canon of love-reading, with Ovid's famous characterization 'quid enim lascivius illa?'. Name and judgment verbatim; literary-canon fact.

pairs.source_text: Et teneri possis carmen legisse Properti, Sive aliquid Galli, sive, Tibulle, tuum:
pairs.question: Quos tres poetas elegiacos Latinos Ovidius puellis legendos commendat?
pairs.question_en: Which three Latin elegiac poets does Ovid recommend that girls read?
pairs.derivation: The Latin elegiac canon as Ovid gives it — tender Propertius, Gallus, Tibullus — all three named verbatim in the reading list. Literary-history fact.

pairs.source_text: Dictaque Varroni fulvis insignia villis Vellera, germanae, Phrixe, querenda tuae:
pairs.question: Quis poeta Latinus vellera fulvis villis insignia, id est Argonautarum fabulam, cecinit?
pairs.question_en: Which Latin poet sang of the fleece famed for its tawny wool — that is, the Argonauts' story?
pairs.derivation: Varro Atacinus and his Argonautica ('the fleece told by Varro'), in the reading list; the golden fleece and Helle ('germanae Phrixe... tuae') anchor the subject. Name verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Et profugum Aenean, altae primordia Romae, Quo nullum Latio clarius extat opus.
pairs.question: Quod carmen Ovidius laudat, 'quo nullum Latio clarius extat opus'?
pairs.question_en: Which poem does Ovid praise as 'the most famous work that exists in Latium'?
pairs.answer_en: Vergil's Aeneid (the poem of the exiled Aeneas).
pairs.derivation: Ovid's celebrated verdict on the Aeneid — 'fugitive Aeneas, the beginnings of high Rome, than which no brighter work stands in Latium'. The subject-description is verbatim; the work's identity is canonical.

pairs.source_text: Deve tribus libris, titulus quos signat Amorum, Elige, quod docili molliter ore legas:
pairs.question: Quot libris opus Ovidii, quod titulus Amorum signat, comprehenditur?
pairs.question_en: In how many books is Ovid's work marked by the title 'Amores' contained?
pairs.derivation: The Amores in three books (the second edition, as its own epigram also records) — Ovid's self-reference, verbatim ('de tribus libris, titulus quos signat Amorum').

pairs.source_text: Vel tibi composita cantetur Epistola voce: Ignotum hoc aliis ille novavit opus.
pairs.question: Quod genus operis Ovidius, aliis ignotum, se primum novavisse gloriatur?
pairs.question_en: What kind of work, unknown to others, does Ovid boast that he first devised?
pairs.derivation: Ovid's claim to have invented the fictional verse-epistle ('ignotum hoc aliis ille novavit opus') — the Heroides as a new genre. Literary-history fact, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Cautaque non stulte latronum proelia ludat, Unus cum gemino calculus hoste perit,
pairs.question: Quo modo calculus in ludo latronum perit?
pairs.answer: Cum gemino hoste deprehensus (inter duos hostes clausus).
pairs.question_en: How is a piece lost in the game of latrunculi ('the robbers')?
pairs.answer_en: When caught by a twin enemy (shut between two enemy pieces).
pairs.derivation: An actual rule of latrunculi: capture by enclosure between two enemy pieces ('unus cum gemino calculus hoste perit'). Gaming realia, verbatim — the rarest kind of spectacle-and-leisure fact.

pairs.source_text: Est genus, in totidem tenui ratione redactum Scriptula, quot menses lubricus annus habet:
pairs.question: In quot scriptula redactum erat genus illud tabulae lusoriae, de quo Ovidius ait totidem esse quot menses annus habet?
pairs.question_en: Into how many lines was that board game divided, of which Ovid says there are as many as the year has months?
pairs.derivation: The ludus duodecim scriptorum: its twelve 'scriptula' matched to the twelve months — the number is Ovid's own aition-like description, verbatim in substance.

pairs.source_text: Parva tabella capit ternos utrimque lapillos, In qua vicisse est continuasse suos.
pairs.question: Quot lapillos utrimque capit parva illa tabella lusoria, in qua vicisse est suos continuasse?
pairs.question_en: How many pebbles a side does that little game-board hold, on which winning is getting one's own in a row?
pairs.derivation: The three-pebble alignment game (a Roman 'three men's morris'): three counters a side, victory by making a line ('vicisse est continuasse suos'). Both rule-facts verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Nec vos Campus habet, nec vos gelidissima Virgo, Nec Tuscus placida devehit amnis aqua.
pairs.question: Quae aqua Romae gelidissima habebatur, qua iuvenes se abluebant?
pairs.question_en: Which water at Rome was held the very coldest, in which the young men bathed?
pairs.derivation: The Aqua Virgo, Agrippa's aqueduct, proverbially icy ('gelidissima Virgo') and the bathing-water of the Campus set — urban realia named verbatim; women are excluded from the Campus, the Virgo, and the Tiber.

pairs.source_text: Nec vos Campus habet, nec vos gelidissima Virgo, Nec Tuscus placida devehit amnis aqua.
pairs.question: Qui amnis Romae 'Tuscus' a poetis dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Which river at Rome is called 'the Tuscan stream' by the poets?
pairs.derivation: The Tiber as 'Tuscus amnis' — the standard poetic epithet from its Etruscan bank/source. The periphrasis has one referent; here the swimming-river of the Campus set.

pairs.source_text: Visite laurigero sacrata Palatia Phoebo: Ille Paraetonicas mersit in alta rates;
pairs.question: Cuius gentis rates Phoebus, cui Palatia sacrata sunt, in alta mersisse dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Whose ships is Phoebus, to whom the Palatine is consecrated, said to have sunk in the deep?
pairs.derivation: The Palatine temple of Apollo as the Actium memorial: the god 'sank the Paraetonian ships' (Paraetonium = the Egyptian port, i.e. Cleopatra's fleet). Monument-and-victory fact verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quaeque soror coniunxque ducis monimenta pararunt, Navalique gener cinctus honore caput;
pairs.question: Quo honore caput generi Augusti, M. Agrippae, cinctum erat?
pairs.question_en: With what honor was the head of Augustus' son-in-law, Agrippa, wreathed?
pairs.answer_en: With the naval one (the naval crown).
pairs.derivation: Agrippa, 'the son-in-law crowned with the naval honor' — the corona navalis he uniquely received; his portico among the strolling-monuments with those of the leader's sister (Octavia) and wife (Livia). Periphrasis with one referent; verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quaeque soror coniunxque ducis monimenta pararunt, Navalique gener cinctus honore caput;
pairs.question: Quae soror ducis Augusti monimenta sua, porticum celebrem, Romae paravit?
pairs.question_en: Which sister of the leader Augustus provided her own monument, the famous portico, at Rome?
pairs.derivation: The Porticus Octaviae among the promenades Ovid lists: 'the monuments the sister of the dux prepared' — the sister of Augustus is Octavia, the canonical referent; the wife's are Livia's (already paired in book I).

pairs.source_text: Visite turicremas vaccae Memphitidos aras, Visite conspicuis terna theatra locis;
pairs.question: Quot theatra Roma aetate Ovidii conspicuis locis habebat?
pairs.question_en: How many theaters did Rome have in conspicuous places in Ovid's day?
pairs.derivation: The 'terna theatra' — Rome's three permanent theaters (of Pompey, Marcellus, and Balbus) — a datable urban fact stated verbatim in the venue catalogue.

pairs.source_text: Spectentur tepido maculosae sanguine harenae, Metaque ferventi circueunda rota.
pairs.question: Quid aurigae in Circo rota ferventi circueundum erat?
pairs.question_en: What did the charioteer in the Circus have to round with his glowing wheel?
pairs.derivation: The meta, the turning-post skimmed by the 'burning wheel' — the central hazard of the chariot race, verbatim; listed with the blood-stained arena among sights to see.

pairs.source_text: Si Venerem Cous nusquam posuisset Apelles, Mersa sub aequoreis illa lateret aquis.
pairs.question: Quis pictor Cous Venerem ex undis surgentem arte sua posuit?
pairs.question_en: Which Coan painter set forth Venus rising from the waves by his art?
pairs.derivation: Apelles of Cos and his Venus (Anadyomene): without him 'she would still lie sunk beneath the sea-water'. Painter, origin, and subject verbatim; the most famous painting of antiquity.

pairs.source_text: Ennius emeruit, Calabris in montibus ortus, Contiguus poni, Scipio magne, tibi.
pairs.question: Ubi natus est Ennius poeta?
pairs.question_en: Where was the poet Ennius born?
pairs.derivation: Ennius' Calabrian origin (Rudiae) — biographical fact of the shared literary tradition, verbatim ('Calabris in montibus ortus').

pairs.source_text: Ennius emeruit, Calabris in montibus ortus, Contiguus poni, Scipio magne, tibi.
pairs.question: Iuxta cuius viri monumentum Ennius poeta poni meruit?
pairs.question_en: Next to which great man's monument did the poet Ennius earn a place?
pairs.derivation: The tradition that Ennius was honored at the tomb of the Scipios ('contiguus poni, Scipio magne, tibi') — the celebrated poet-and-patron fact, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Quis Danaen nosset, si semper clusa fuisset, Inque sua turri perlatuisset anus?
pairs.question: Quo inclusa servabatur Danae?
pairs.question_en: In what was Danae kept shut away?
pairs.derivation: Danae imprisoned in her tower (where Jupiter came as the golden shower) — canonical myth-fact, verbatim ('in sua turri'); Ovid's point about fame is the frame.

pairs.source_text: Ad multas lupa tendit oves, praedetur ut unam, Et Iovis in multas devolat ales aves.
pairs.question: Quae avis 'Iovis ales' apud poetas Romanos dicitur?
pairs.question_en: Which bird is called 'the bird of Jove' by the Roman poets?
pairs.derivation: The eagle as Jupiter's bird — here the predator swooping on many birds; the periphrasis 'Iovis ales' presupposes the canonical identification asked. Shared attribute-lore.

pairs.source_text: Funere saepe viri vir quaeritur; ire solutis Crinibus et fletus non tenuisse decet.
pairs.question: Quo capillorum habitu feminae Romanae in funere ire solebant?
pairs.question_en: With their hair in what state did Roman women customarily go at a funeral?
pairs.derivation: Mourning custom: women at funerals with unbound hair and open weeping ('ire solutis crinibus et fletus non tenuisse decet') — the funerary realia kept, the cynical husband-hunting frame dropped.

pairs.source_text: Vix mihi credetis, sed credite: Troia maneret, Praeceptis Priamo si foret usa satae.
pairs.question: Quae Priamo sata vera de Troia monuit, cuius praeceptis si usa esset, Troia maneret?
pairs.question_en: Which daughter of Priam gave true warnings about Troy, by whose counsels, had they been heeded, Troy would still stand?
pairs.derivation: Cassandra the unheeded prophetess — 'Troy would remain, had it used the counsels of Priam's daughter'. The periphrasis 'satae Priamo' has the one canonical referent; the unbelieved-prophecy fact is verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Et tibi, Demophoon, Thesei criminis heres, Phyllide decepta nulla relicta fides.
pairs.question: Cuius herois filius et 'criminis heres' erat Demophoon, qui Phyllida decepit?
pairs.question_en: Of which hero was Demophoon the son and 'heir of his crime', he who deceived Phyllis?
pairs.derivation: Demophoon as Theseus' son, repeating his father's desertion (Theseus left Ariadne; Demophoon left Phyllis) — 'Thesei criminis heres' verbatim; completes the Phyllis pair.

pairs.source_text: Verba vadum temptent abiegnis scripta tabellis: Accipiat missas apta ministra notas.
pairs.question: E qua materia ligni tabellae scriptoriae fiebant, ut Ovidius significat?
pairs.question_en: Of what wood were writing-tablets made, as Ovid indicates?
pairs.derivation: Letter-realia: the fir-wood tabellae ('abiegnis... tabellis') carried by the trusted maid ('apta ministra') — complements the wax-tablet pair of book I.

pairs.source_text: Dux bonus huic centum commisit vite regendos, Huic equites, illi signa tuenda dedit:
pairs.question: Quot milites viti (centurionis insigni) regendos dux bonus commisit?
pairs.question_en: How many soldiers did a good general entrust to the vine-staff (the centurion's emblem) to command?
pairs.derivation: The centurion: a hundred men ruled 'by the vitis', the vine-staff that was his badge of rank — Roman military institution stated verbatim ('centum commisit vite regendos').

pairs.source_text: Odimus et maestas: Tecmessam diligat Aiax; Nos hilarem populum femina laeta capit.
pairs.question: Cuius herois contubernalis et amata erat Tecmessa?
pairs.question_en: Of which hero was Tecmessa the captive consort and beloved?
pairs.derivation: Tecmessa, the sorrowful captive-bride of Ajax (of Sophocles' play), cited as the type of the gloomy woman. Both names verbatim; canonical pairing.

pairs.source_text: Nos facimus placitae late praeconia formae: Nomen habet Nemesis, Cynthia nomen habet: Vesper et Eoae novere Lycorida terrae:
pairs.question: Quas tres puellas carmina poetarum elegiacorum nobilitaverunt, teste Ovidio?
pairs.question_en: Which three women did the songs of the elegiac poets make famous, on Ovid's testimony?
pairs.derivation: The celebrated elegiac mistresses — Nemesis (Tibullus'), Cynthia (Propertius'), Lycoris (Gallus', known 'to Evening and the Eastern lands') — all three named verbatim as fame made by poets.

pairs.source_text: Vesper et Eoae novere Lycorida terrae: Et multi, quae sit nostra Corinna, rogant.
pairs.question: Quo nomine puella ab Ovidio ipso in carminibus amatoriis celebrata vocatur?
pairs.question_en: By what name is the woman celebrated by Ovid himself in his love-poems called?
pairs.derivation: Ovid's own Corinna, of the Amores, named beside Nemesis, Cynthia, and Lycoris — 'many ask who my Corinna is'. Self-referential literary fact, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Tuta quoque est fallitque oculos e lacte recenti Littera: carbonis pulvere tange, leges.
pairs.question: Quo liquore litterae occultae scribebantur, quae carbonis pulvere tactae legi possent?
pairs.question_en: With what liquid were secret letters written, which could be read when touched with charcoal dust?
pairs.derivation: Invisible-ink realia: writing in fresh milk, developed by dusting with powdered charcoal — both the medium and the developer verbatim. A hard, checkable practice-fact of letter culture.

pairs.source_text: Adfuit Acrisio servandae cura puellae: Hunc tamen illa suo crimine fecit avum.
pairs.question: Quem Danae, quamvis servata, suo crimine avum fecit?
pairs.question_en: Whom did Danae, though closely guarded, make a grandfather by her fault?
pairs.derivation: Acrisius, Danae's jailer-father, made grandfather (of Perseus) despite the guard — the canonical point of the story, both names verbatim; completes the tower pair.

pairs.source_text: Cum sedeat Phariae sistris operata iuvencae, Quoque sui comites ire vetantur, eat,
pairs.question: Quo instrumento sacra Phariae iuvencae Isidis celebrabantur?
pairs.question_en: With what instrument were the rites of the Pharian heifer, Isis, celebrated?
pairs.derivation: The sistrum, the rattle of Isis' cult ('Phariae sistris operata iuvencae') — Egyptian-rite realia at Rome, verbatim; distinct from the temple-venue pairs of book I.

pairs.source_text: Cum, custode foris tunicas servante puellae, Celent furtivos balnea multa iocos,
pairs.question: Quid custos ante balnea servabat, dum domina intus lavabatur?
pairs.question_en: What did the attendant guard outside the baths while his mistress bathed within?
pairs.derivation: Bath realia: the slave posted outside to watch the clothes (clothes-theft at the baths was proverbial) while the baths hid much else. Verbatim ('custode foris tunicas servante').

pairs.source_text: Fallitur et multo custodis cura Lyaeo, Illa vel Hispano lecta sit uva iugo;
pairs.question: Unde uva vini vilioris legebatur, quo custodes inebriari poterant, ut Ovidius ait?
pairs.question_en: From where came the grapes of the cheaper wine with which watchmen could be made drunk, as Ovid says?
pairs.derivation: Spanish hill-wine as the cheap plentiful drink at Rome ('vel Hispano lecta... uva iugo') — wine-trade realia verbatim; the guard-tricking advice dropped.

pairs.source_text: Munera, crede mihi, capiunt hominesque deosque: Placatur donis Iuppiter ipse datis.
pairs.question: Quos munera capere ait Ovidius sententia celebri?
pairs.question_en: Whom does Ovid say, in a famous maxim, that gifts win over?
pairs.answer_en: Both men and gods (Jupiter himself is appeased by gifts).
pairs.derivation: 'Munera capiunt hominesque deosque' — the quotable maxim on the power of gifts, its point verbatim and attributed to Ovid.

pairs.source_text: Viderit utilitas: ego coepta fideliter edam: Lemniasin gladios in mea fata dabo.
pairs.question: Quo facinore Lemniades, quibus Ovidius se gladios in sua fata dare ait, notae sunt?
pairs.question_en: For what deed were the Lemnian women notorious, to whom Ovid says he hands swords for his own destruction?
pairs.derivation: The Lemnian women's man-slaughter — the canonical crime Ovid's self-ironic image presupposes ('Lemniasin gladios in mea fata dabo'). Shared Argonautic-background story.

pairs.source_text: Est prope purpureos colles florentis Hymetti Fons sacer et viridi caespite mollis humus:
pairs.question: Prope quem montem Atticum fons ille sacer erat, ubi Cephalus lassus requiescere solebat?
pairs.question_en: Near which Attic mountain was the sacred spring where the weary Cephalus used to rest?
pairs.derivation: The setting of the Cephalus-Procris tragedy: the sacred spring by the flowering, purple hills of Hymettus. Place-fact verbatim, opening the inset.

pairs.source_text: Ecce, redit Cephalus silvis, Cyllenia proles, Oraque fontana fervida pulsat aqua.
pairs.question: Cuius dei proles erat Cephalus, quem 'Cyllenia proles' Ovidius vocat?
pairs.question_en: Of which god was Cephalus the offspring, whom Ovid calls 'the Cyllenian's child'?
pairs.derivation: Cephalus as son of Mercury ('Cyllenia proles', from Mercury's birth-mountain Cyllene) — genealogical fact in the epithet, canonical identification.

pairs.source_text: Procris ut accepit nomen, quasi paelicis, Aurae, Excidit, et subito muta dolore fuit;
pairs.question: Quod nomen Procris quasi paelicis accepit, cum Cephalus auram tantum vocaret?
pairs.question_en: What name did Procris take to be a rival's, when Cephalus was only calling on the breeze?
pairs.derivation: The pivot of the Cephalus-Procris story: 'Aura', the breeze he invoked to cool him, misheard as a mistress's name. Verbatim ('nomen, quasi paelicis, Aurae'); canonical tale (Met. 7 not yet mined).

pairs.source_text: Ille feram movisse ratus, iuvenaliter artus Corripit, in dextra tela fuere manu. Quid facis, infelix? non est fera, supprime tela! Me miserum! iaculo fixa puella tuo est.
pairs.question: Quo modo Procris a Cephalo coniuge perempta est?
pairs.answer: Iaculo eius fixa, cum ille feram movisse ratus esset.
pairs.question_en: How was Procris killed by her husband Cephalus?
pairs.answer_en: Pierced by his javelin, when he thought a wild beast had stirred the leaves.
pairs.derivation: The canonical death of Procris: hidden in the brush, mistaken for a beast, struck by Cephalus' own javelin ('feram movisse ratus... iaculo fixa puella'). Cause and weapon verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Exit, et incauto paulatim pectore lapsus Excipitur miseri spiritus ore viri.
pairs.question: Quo Cephalus animam morientis Procridis excepit?
pairs.question_en: With what did Cephalus receive the departing breath of the dying Procris?
pairs.derivation: The last breath caught in the husband's mouth — the closing image of the inset, mirroring the Roman custom of catching a dying kin's final breath with a kiss. Verbatim ('excipitur... spiritus ore viri').

pairs.source_text: Carpe cibos digitis: est quiddam gestus edendi: Ora nec immunda tota perungue manu.
pairs.question: Quibus cibi in mensa Romana carpebantur?
pairs.question_en: With what was food taken at the Roman table?
pairs.derivation: Table realia: Romans ate with their fingers, and there was an art to the gesture ('est quiddam gestus edendi') — the fork-less table as shared custom, verbatim.

pairs.source_text: Sed neque Phoebei tripodes nec corniger Ammon Vera magis vobis, quam mea Musa, canet:
pairs.question: Quis deus fatidicus 'corniger' a poetis dicitur, cuius oraculum cum tripodibus Phoebi confertur?
pairs.question_en: Which oracular god is called 'horned' by the poets, his oracle ranked with the tripods of Phoebus?
pairs.derivation: The ram-horned Ammon of the Libyan oracle, paired with Delphi's tripods as the two great truth-speakers. Epithet and pairing verbatim; canonical iconography.

pairs.source_text: Ut quondam iuvenes, ita nunc, mea turba, puellae Inscribant spoliis 'Naso magister erat.'
pairs.question: Quae verba discipulos suos spoliis inscribere Ovidius in fine Artis iubet?
pairs.question_en: What words does Ovid, at the end of the Ars, bid his pupils inscribe on their spoils?
pairs.derivation: The famous closing tag of the Ars (ending books II and III alike): the victors' dedication 'Naso magister erat'. Proverb-famous quotation whose point (whose words, where placed) is checkable; verbatim.
